adesso: Honour them at life’s great passages — a birth, a bereavement, a decisive turn — recognising what is in your hands and what is not. Cultivate the serenity to accept the inevitable, distinguishing it from the courage to act where you can still choose. Light a candle and honour your ancestors, remembering that you are part of a thread that comes from far away. They are patrons of awareness of time and of the weight of choices.

intro: Nike is the winged goddess who descends to crown the one who triumphs, swift as a beat of wings and bright as glory itself. Daughter of the Titan Pallas and of the marsh Styx, together with her siblings Zelos, Kratos and Bia she took Zeus’s side in the war against the Titans, and for this the king of the gods kept her forever beside him. Tradition remembers her as the charioteer of his chariot and his inseparable companion, so that she often appears in the very hand of Zeus or of Athena, a small figure holding out the crown to the victor. She flies over battlefields and stadiums, poised an instant before alighting on the head of one who has earned the triumph, in war as in athletic games and poetic contests. She is not the strength that wins, but the shining and fleeting moment of victory consecrated. The Greeks felt her near in every effort crowned with success, and admired her light grace.
allora: Winged goddess of victory and companion of Athena, Nike crowned the victors of wars and games. Her most famous sanctuary is the temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis of Athens, where she was venerated in her "wingless" form (Aptera), so that victory might never leave the city. Trophies, crowns and songs of triumph were dedicated to her, and her image adorned monuments raised in memory of battles won.
adesso: Invoke her before an important challenge — an exam, a race, an interview, a goal long pursued — asking her for the clarity and the drive to give your best. When you win something, dedicate it to her with gratitude rather than arrogance, remembering how precious and fleeting victory is. A small laurel or a token of your achievement laid on the altar honours her. She is the patron of sport, of determination and of goals attained.

intro: Tyche is the unstable and powerful goddess who holds the rudder of chance, able to raise a person to wealth or overturn them into misery with a single turn of her wheel. Held to be daughter of Ocean or of Zeus, she presides over fortune understood as what happens without merit or fault, the pure unforeseen of luck. In one hand she holds the cornucopia brimming with goods, in the other the rudder with which she steers human affairs, and beneath her foot sometimes the sphere or the wheel, the image of her changeable and never settled nature. She dispenses Eutychia, good luck, but misfortune too, for fortune knows no loyalty. In the Hellenistic age her cult grew enormously: every city wanted its own protecting Tyche, crowned with walls, guarantor of its prosperity. The Greeks felt her wherever destiny showed itself capricious, and knew she was to be treated with respect and without presumption.
allora: Venerated as the giver of fortune and prosperity, Tyche had cult at Pharai, Smyrna, Sikyon, Athens and Olympia, and as the Tyche of a city she became protectress of whole cities, with the mural crown upon her head. She was often paired with Nemesis, who balanced her gifts and prevented excessive fortune from turning into presumption. Libations, first fruits, coins and incense were offered to her, in thanks and in request for her favour.
adesso: Honour her by meeting the changes of fortune with balance, neither exulting in good luck nor despairing in bad. In fortunate moments, offer a small gesture of gratitude — a coin given away, a symbolic offering — recognising that not everything depends on you. Cultivate hope and flexibility in the face of the unforeseen, remembering that the wheel always turns. She is the patron of accepting chance and of trust in the future.

intro: Nemesis is the goddess who watches over the balance of the world and tolerates no excess: her name derives from the verb meaning "to distribute what is due", for it falls to her to give each back their rightful share. Daughter of Night, she embodies divine indignation against presumption, hybris, that boundless pride with which mortals forget their limits and challenge the gods. When someone’s fortune grows beyond measure, or when someone enjoys an undeserved good, it is Nemesis who lowers the scales and brings things back to their order. Winged, with bridle and whip in hand, she pursues whoever runs too high and calls them back to measure. Myth also binds her to the birth of Helen, brought forth from an egg after Zeus pursued her by changing into a swan. The Greeks feared her as the voice that reminds every fortunate person: nothing in excess.
allora: Her most famous sanctuary stood at Rhamnous in Attica, where the statue carved by Agorakritos, a pupil of Phidias, was venerated — made according to tradition from the marble the Persians had brought to raise a monument to the victory they expected, a victory their own hybris turned into defeat. The Nemesia were celebrated there and libations, branches and incense were offered to her. She was often invoked beside Tyche, to temper the excesses of fortune.
adesso: Honour her by cultivating measure, humility and a sense of justice, recognising your limits and resisting the temptation of arrogance. When life smiles on you, remember not to grow proud; when you suffer a wrong, trust to the restoring of balance rather than to blind revenge. A moment of sobriety and measured gratitude is already homage to her. She is the patron of inner balance and of respect for limits.

intro: Eros is the force that kindles passion and moves all things towards union: in the oldest cosmogonies he is one of the first powers born from Chaos, a primordial principle that drives beings to love and to beget. The more widespread tradition, however, makes him the beautiful son of Aphrodite, a winged youth with laughing eyes, armed with a bow and golden arrows with which he pierces the hearts of gods and mortals, and with the torch with which he sets their desire alight. No one is safe from his shafts, and even Zeus must yield to his power; capricious and irresistible, he plays with the fortunes of lovers. His most famous myth binds him to Psyche, the mortal soul he loved in secret and who, after trials and sorrows, was made immortal and his wife forever — a tale of the love that unites desire and soul. The Greeks venerated him as the power that holds the world together and makes life worth living.
allora: The oldest centre of his cult was Thespiai in Boeotia, where Eros was venerated in the form of an unworked stone and the Erotidia were celebrated every four years, festivals with athletic and musical contests in his honour. He was honoured also at Athens, near the Academy, and in the wrestling schools, as a power that inspired both love and valour. Flowers, roses, libations and incense were offered to him, and lovers turned to him.
adesso: Invoke him in relationships of love and whenever you wish to cultivate passion, tenderness and a deep connection with another person. Honour him with flowers, with sincere gestures of affection and with care for your bonds, remembering that love must be nourished and not only desired. A small altar with roses and a candle can accompany your thoughts of the one you love. He is the patron of love, of desire and of the bonds of the heart.

ep: Goddess of the rainbow and messenger
intro: Iris is the goddess who joins sky and earth, appearing as the rainbow that stretches out bright after the rain. Daughter of the Titan Thaumas and the Oceanid Elektra, and sister of the Harpies, she has golden wings and an iridescent robe, and descends swift as light to carry the messages of the Olympian gods to mortals and to the other divinities. She is above all the faithful handmaid of Hera, whose commands she carries out, but she serves all Olympus, crossing in an instant seas, mountains and even the depths of Hades, where she draws the water of the Styx by which the gods pronounce their solemn oaths. Always in motion, she has almost no myths of her own: her essence is transit, the bridge, the bond. Like the rainbow that marks the end of the storm, she brings with her a sense of hope and of reconciliation between the divine and the human. The Greeks saw her every time the sky opened in colour after the rain.
dom: The bond between sky and earth
allora: Messenger of the gods and handmaid of Hera, Iris did not have as widespread a cult as other divinities, but she was honoured in particular at Delos, where the inhabitants offered her wheat cakes kneaded with honey and dried figs. Her figure recurred in poetry and art as a link between the worlds, swift and tireless. The rainbow itself, which bore her name, was felt to be a favourable sign from her.
adesso: Honour her as the carrier of messages and connections: when you have to communicate something difficult, seek reconciliation after a quarrel or bring good news, invoke her to guide your words. She is the goddess of the hope that returns after the storm, so turn to her at times of recovery and of new beginnings. A glass of clear water offered to the light can be her simple homage. She is the patron of messengers, journeys and new beginnings.

intro: Agathos Daimon, the "Good Spirit", is the kindly power that watches over the prosperity of the house and the good fortune of the family. Portrayed as a serpent, the animal that in Greek tradition guards places and the wealth beneath the earth, he is the household spirit above all others, guarantor of abundance and of the protection of the hearth. He has no elaborate myth: his presence is felt in daily life, in the well-being that makes a household serene. He was invoked with affection and familiarity, as a close and discreet protector. To him, at the end of the meal, the first cup of unmixed wine was poured, in a gesture of gratitude for the gifts received. He embodied the idea that every home was watched over by a good spirit, to be honoured so that fortune should not leave the threshold.
off: A libation of unmixed wine after the meal
allora: The "good spirit" of the house was honoured on the second day of every month, dedicated to him, with a libation of pure wine, unmixed with water, poured after the meal. It was customary, once the meal was over, to offer him the first cup in token of thanks and to win good fortune for the family. His serpent image was sometimes painted in houses, in protection of the storeroom and the hearth.
adesso: Honour him with a simple toast of gratitude for your home and for good fortune: the first cup poured or dedicated to him, at the end of a meal, renews the ancient gesture. It is a concrete way of recognising and cultivating the well-being of the place you live in and of the people who share it. A grateful thought before sitting down at table, or at the end of dinner, is enough to make it a daily rite. He is the discreet patron of household prosperity.

ep: Hero of strength, warder-off of evils
intro: Heracles is the greatest of the Greek heroes, son of Zeus and the mortal Alkmene, whose whole existence was marked by Hera’s hatred and by the labour of atoning for and overcoming trials. In a fit of madness sent by the goddess he killed his own children, and to purify himself he submitted to the service of King Eurystheus, performing the famous Twelve Labours: he killed the Nemean lion and the Hydra of Lerna, captured the Cerynean hind and the Erymanthian boar, cleaned the stables of Augeas, tamed the bull of Crete and the mares of Diomedes, won the belt of the Amazon and the cattle of Geryon, gathered the apples of the Hesperides and dragged Cerberus out of Hades. His strength was immense, but greater still was his capacity to endure and persevere. He died in flames, poisoned by the robe of the centaur Nessus, but the fire burned away only the mortal part and Zeus received him among the gods. For this he was venerated with a double nature, hero and divinity at once.
sim: The skin of the Nemean lion
off: Double sacrifices: part as to a god, part as to a hero
Roasted meats at the sacred banquet
allora: Alone among the heroes, Heracles received a cult of double nature: in some places heroic and chthonic sacrifices were offered to him, poured onto the ground for the dead beneath, in others divine honours as to an Olympian god. The oldest centre of the cult was Thebes, his native city, but sanctuaries, altars and games dedicated to him rose all over Greece. As Alexikakos, "he who wards off evils", he was invoked in defence of houses and cities against misfortune.
adesso: Invoke him as patron of strength, resilience and perseverance in the face of the "labours" of daily life, those trials that seem never to end. When you face a difficulty that demands tenacity, ask him for the courage to go on one step at a time. An altar with the club or the lion skin and a libation of wine suits the request for inner strength. He is the patron of those who do not give up.

intro: Theseus is the hero Athens chose as its champion and symbol, son of King Aegeus (or of the god Poseidon) and of Aithra. Raised far from his father, as soon as he was strong enough to lift the rock under which his father’s sword and sandals lay hidden, he set out for Athens by the dangerous land route, ridding the isthmus of brigands and monsters such as Procrustes and Periphetes, whose club he took. But his most famous exploit was the descent into the Labyrinth of Crete, where he killed the Minotaur and came out again thanks to the thread Ariadne had given him. Returning to Athens, he forgot to raise the white sails, and his father Aegeus, believing him dead, threw himself into the sea. Having become king, Theseus united Attica into a single state by the synoecism and was remembered as the founder of the city and the first guarantor of its institutions. His figure embodied civic courage and the defence of the weak.
dom: Defence of the young and the oppressed
off: Sacrifices on the 8th of every month (a number sacred to him, as to Poseidon)
Chthonic offerings poured onto the ground
allora: After his death Theseus was honoured as the protecting hero of Athens; the general Kimon, following an oracle, brought back from the island of Skyros what were believed to be his bones and raised him the Theseion, which became a sacred asylum for slaves and the oppressed seeking refuge. The Theseia were celebrated in his honour, with sacrifices and games, and heroic rites were offered to him on the eighth day of every month, a number sacred to him and to Poseidon. He was felt to be the very patron of Athenian identity.
adesso: Honour him as patron of justice, of civic courage and of the defence of the weakest, and invoke him when you must take a stand for what is right. He is also the ideal guide in inner "labyrinths": ask him for the thread that helps you find your bearings in difficult choices and find the way out. A concrete act of solidarity towards someone in difficulty is the most genuine way of honouring him. He gives you the strength to face trials with a sense of community.

intro: Perseus is the hero who defeated the impossible and faced the gaze that turns to stone, son of Zeus and of Danaë, the princess the god reached in the form of a shower of gold. Shut as a newborn into a chest cast into the sea together with his mother, he was saved and grew up on the island of Seriphos, until King Polydektes, to be rid of him, sent him on an errand that seemed certain death: to bring back the head of Medusa, the Gorgon whose gaze turned every living being to stone. Helped by Athena and Hermes, he obtained the winged sandals, the helm of invisibility of Hades and the adamantine sickle, and managed to behead Medusa by looking only at her reflection on his polished shield. On the way back, with the head that still petrified, he freed Andromeda, chained to a rock as prey for a sea monster, and took her as his wife. The Gorgon’s head, given to Athena, became the apotropaic emblem above all others. His story taught how to defeat fear with cunning and courage.
dom: Courage in the face of fear
Protection against evil and the evil eye
off: Chthonic offerings poured onto the ground
allora: Perseus was venerated as a hero at Seriphos, at Mycenae — the city tradition credited him with founding — at Argos and at Athens, where heroa were dedicated to him. The Gorgon’s head, the Gorgoneion, became a most powerful apotropaic symbol, carved on doors, shields, walls and coins to drive off evil and the evil eye. Sacrifices and votive gifts were offered to him in the heroa, according to the rites due to a hero.
adesso: Honour him as patron of courage and protection: you may keep an image of the Gorgoneion as an amulet against negative energies and fears. Invoke him above all when you face a fear that paralyses you, remembering that he did not look the monster in the face, but knew how to confront it by cunning, in reflection. Ask him for the clarity not to let yourself be turned to stone by fear, but to find the way past it. He is the patron of those who defeat what seems unbeatable.

intro: Asklepios is the great healer, son of Apollo and the mortal Koronis, whose medical art was so perfect that it crossed the very bounds of life. Snatched still in the womb from his dying mother upon the pyre, he was entrusted to the wise centaur Cheiron, who taught him the secrets of herbs and of medicine. Becoming a physician without equal, he even learned to raise the dead — thanks, it is said, to the Gorgon’s blood given him by Athena — and this disturbed the order of the cosmos: Zeus, fearing that mortals might escape death, struck him with the thunderbolt. But afterwards, to make amends or to acknowledge his merits, he raised him among the stars and among the gods, making him the power of medicine. His staff with the serpent coiled about it is still today the symbol of the medical art. Father of daughters such as Hygieia (Health) and Panakeia, he was the hope of every sick person in the ancient world.
off: Incubation: sleeping in the temple for a healing dream
Votive offerings of healed body parts
allora: The cult of Asklepios had its most famous centre at Epidauros, and from there spread to the Asklepieia of Kos, Pergamon, Athens and the whole Greek world. Its most characteristic rite was incubation: the sick slept within the sacred precinct hoping the god would appear to them in a dream to indicate the cure or to heal them directly. Those who were healed offered votive images of the mended parts of the body and sacrificed a cockerel, as even Socrates recalls in his last words.
adesso: He is the patron of health above all others: invoke him before an operation, during an illness, or for the healing of someone dear to you. You may dedicate a small offering to him before falling asleep, asking for dreams that show you the way to healing, of body or of spirit. An act of care towards yourself or towards someone ill is already a way of honouring him. He stands for the hope of healing and the art of those who care.

intro: The Dioskouroi, Kastor and Polydeukes, are the shining twins who rush to save those in danger, at sea and in battle. Sons of Leda, they were born of a singular circumstance: Polydeukes, begotten by Zeus, was immortal, while Kastor, son of the mortal Tyndareos, was destined to die. Raised together, Kastor excelled at breaking horses and Polydeukes at boxing, and they took part in great enterprises, such as the hunt of the Calydonian boar and the expedition of the Argonauts. When Kastor fell in a feud, Polydeukes, in despair, would not enjoy immortality alone and begged Zeus to share his own lot with his brother: so the two twins alternate their existence, one day among the gods of Olympus, one day in the darkness of Hades. Changed at last into the constellation of the Twins, they appear to sailors as St Elmo’s fire, twin lights that announce salvation. They are the purest image of brotherly love and faithfulness.
dom: Protection at sea and on journeys
off: Theoxenia: a banquet with a table laid to receive them as guests
allora: Their cult was born at Sparta, where they were venerated as protectors of the city and symbolised by the dokana, two beams of wood joined together, and it spread afterwards through the whole Greek and Roman world. They were honoured with the Theoxenia, sacred banquets at which a table was laid to receive them as divine guests. They appeared to sailors in storms as twin lights of salvation and to horsemen in battle on white horses, and received sacrifices in harbours and hippodromes.
adesso: They are the ideal patrons of travellers: invoke them before setting out, for safety by air, by road or by sea, and for those you love who are far from home. You may light two twin lights and offer a symbolic meal, in the spirit of the ancient Theoxenia, as a sign of hospitality and a request for protection. Turn to them also to strengthen brotherly bonds and faithful friendships. They watch over wayfarers and over those who support one another.

intro: Achilles is the warrior without equal of the Trojan War, son of the mortal Peleus and of the sea goddess Thetis, who tried to make him invulnerable by dipping him in the waters of the Styx, holding him by the heel that thus remained his only weak point. He knew, by prophecy, that he had to choose between a long and obscure life and a short but glorious one, and he chose glory. The Iliad is born of his wrath: insulted by King Agamemnon, who took from him the captive Briseis, he withdrew from the battle, and only the death of his beloved companion Patroklos, killed by Hektor, brought him back raging to the field. He avenged his friend by killing Hektor and dragged his body around the walls, until old King Priam came to beg him to give back his son’s corpse, in one of the most moving scenes of the poem. Achilles himself fell soon after, struck in the heel by an arrow of Paris guided by Apollo. He embodied absolute valour and the tragic awareness of mortality.
dom: Protection of those who sail the Black Sea
off: Night sacrifices at the burial mound
Libations of wine, honey and milk poured onto the ground
allora: A half-divine hero, Achilles was venerated at the mound of Sigeion, near Troy, where sailors stopped to pay him honour, and above all as lord of the White Island, Leuke, in the Black Sea, where tradition held he had been carried after death to live a second heroic existence. He received night sacrifices and holocausts, victims wholly burned according to the chthonic rite, and funeral games in his honour. The sailors of the Euxine invoked him as protector of their routes.
adesso: Honour him as patron of valour and of excellence, the arete the Greeks admired above all things, and invoke him when you face a challenge that demands absolute courage and total dedication. A libation at sunset, poured onto the ground, can accompany the request for inner strength and for faithfulness to friends, virtues dear to him until death. Remember his tragic lesson too: glory has a price, and faithfulness to those we love counts for more than victory. He is the patron of those who give all of themselves.

ep: Divine singer and master of the mysteries
intro: Orpheus is the singer whose music had power over the whole world, son of the Muse Kalliope and of a Thracian king, or of Apollo himself. When he took up the lyre and sang, wild beasts grew tame, trees bent down, stones moved and even rivers stopped to listen. He took part in the expedition of the Argonauts, and with his song overcame the deadly call of the Sirens. But the myth that made him immortal is that of Eurydice, his beloved wife dead of a serpent’s bite: Orpheus went down alive into Hades and with his music moved even Hades and Persephone, who granted him to bring her back to the light, provided he did not turn to look at her before going out. At the last step, overcome by the anxiety of love, he turned, and lost her forever. Torn with grief, he died dismembered by the Maenads, but his head went on singing and prophesying. He became the legendary founder of the Orphic mysteries, master of a path of purification of the soul.
off: Honey, milk and water (refusal of blood sacrifice)
allora: A Thracian singer, Orpheus was held to be the founder of the Orphic mysteries, a religious current that taught a doctrine of the soul, of its fall into the body and of its purification through rites and a life of abstinence. His head, according to legend, floated as far as Lesbos, where it went on prophesying from an oracle. The Orphics followed purifications, refused blood sacrifice and offered bloodless libations of honey, milk and water, accompanied by sung hymns.
adesso: He is the patron of musicians, poets and of anyone seeking an inner, spiritual path. Honour him with music, with the singing of hymns and with meditation, asking him for inspiration and guidance in the growth of the soul. Turn to him also in bereavement, for he knew the most painful loss and made song of it: his story teaches how to turn grief into beauty. A moment of recollection with the music you love is already homage to him.

intro: Bellerophon is the hero who tamed the winged horse and faced an unbeatable monster, a prince of Corinth, son of Glaukos (or of the god Poseidon). His most famous exploit was taming Pegasus, the winged horse born from the blood of Medusa, which he achieved thanks to the golden bridle given him by the goddess Athena, who appeared to him in a dream. Mounted on Pegasus he faced the Chimaera, the fire-vomiting monster with the body of a lion, the tail of a serpent and the head of a goat, and killed it from above by driving into its throat a spear tipped with lead, which the beast’s own fire melted and so choked it. He performed other victorious deeds for the king of Lycia, who had laid those deadly traps for him, and in the end married his daughter. But good fortune made him proud: he wished to rise into the sky with Pegasus as far as the dwelling of the gods, and Zeus, to punish his presumption, made the horse rear. Bellerophon fell and ended his days blind and alone, wandering in disgrace. His story is at once a triumph and a warning.
off: Sacrifices and libations in the temenos at Corinth
Chthonic offerings poured onto the ground
allora: Bellerophon was venerated as a hero at Corinth, his homeland, where a sacred precinct was dedicated to him in the grove of Kraneion, and honoured also in Lycia, the scene of his exploits. At Corinth Athena Chalinitis, "of the bridle", was venerated in memory of the golden bridle with which the hero had tamed Pegasus, and votive gifts were offered to her. Heroic sacrifices and libations were rendered to him, according to the rites due to heroes.
adesso: Honour him as patron of ambitious courage and of mastery over your own powers, invoking him before an undertaking that seems beyond you. His story teaches that, with the right help and determination, even the most frightening "chimaeras" can be defeated. But always remember the warning of his fall: do not let success turn into boundless pride. He gives you the drive to dare, and the wisdom to know your limits.

intro: Atalanta is the untameable heroine who chose the freedom of the woods, abandoned at birth by a father who wanted a son and suckled by a she-bear sent by Artemis. Raised wild among hunters, she became swift and strong as no man was, vowed to virginity after the example of the goddess. When the giant Calydonian boar was laying waste the countryside, she joined the greatest heroes in the hunt and it was she who first wounded the beast, drawing its first blood and earning the trophy, which her admirer Meleager granted her. In running she was unbeatable, and to escape marriage she imposed a deadly contest on her suitors: whoever beat her would marry her, whoever lost would die. No one outran her, until Hippomenes (or Melanion), with Aphrodite’s help, let three golden apples fall along the course: Atalanta stopped to gather them and lost the race, and with it her freedom. Her story celebrates female strength and self-determination.
off: Votive offerings from the hunt (often with Artemis)
Libations and gifts at sacred places
allora: Atalanta’s figure was closely bound to the cult of Artemis, the virgin goddess of the hunt whose wild and free spirit she embodied. Remembered for the Calydonian hunt and for her running contests, she was honoured in places of Arcadia and Boeotia, which disputed her origin, with votive offerings from the hunt and first fruits. Her image recurred in art as a model of female athletic strength and courage.
adesso: She is the patron of women athletes, of hunters, and of anyone who defends their independence and their own nature. Invoke her for physical strength, for fair competition and for the courage not to betray who you are, even when the world would have you otherwise. Her story is a reminder of how precious it is to stay faithful to your freedom and not to be distracted by "golden apples" that make us lose the race. She gives you determination and pride.

intro: Jason is the hero who managed to gather the greatest champions of Greece into a single undertaking, a Thessalian prince deprived of the throne of Iolkos by his usurping uncle Pelias. Raised in secret by the centaur Cheiron, he returned to claim the kingdom, and along the way, having lost a sandal while helping an old woman — the goddess Hera in disguise — he presented himself wearing only one, fulfilling an oracle Pelias feared. His uncle, to be rid of him, imposed on him the apparently impossible mission of bringing back the Golden Fleece from far-off Colchis. Jason had the ship Argo built and gathered a crew of legendary heroes — the Argonauts, among them Heracles, Orpheus, the Dioskouroi and Atalanta — facing a thousand dangers with them: the Symplegades, the Harpies, hostile peoples. In Colchis he won the Fleece thanks to the help of the sorceress Medea, the king’s daughter, who fell in love with him and saved him from deadly trials. His name remains bound to the courage of the collective undertaking and to the voyage that opened up the world.
off: Libations and heroic sacrifices for a favourable voyage
Offerings to the sea divinities before departure
allora: The legend of Jason and the Argonauts was among the oldest and best loved in Greece, and it traced in imagination the routes of Greek navigation and settlement in the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Many cities and places along the coasts preserved memories and cults connected with the passage of the ship Argo and its heroes. Libations and heroic sacrifices were rendered to him, and before departures by sea the sea divinities were honoured, as sailors did in memory of that first great expedition.
adesso: Honour him as patron of shared projects, of journeys and of teamwork, invoking him when you must begin an undertaking no one could accomplish alone. His story teaches that the success of a great project depends on knowing how to gather the right people and lead them through the trials. Ask him for the ability to inspire and coordinate those at your side towards a common goal. He is the patron of those who set sail together.
